newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan shippers anxious over post-handover links with HK.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan shippers anxious over post-handover links with HK.

text.p: Anxiety is growing in Taiwan's shipping industry over the island's relationship with Hong Kong after the British colony is absorbed by communist China in July.

Hong Kong is a key transhipment point for Taiwan goods sold to China and, despite an unwritten agreement it will be business as usual after the handover, Taiwan fears arch-rival Beijing may exercise its new clout to coax it into rejoining the mainland after a 48-year separation.

Without a signed technical agreement the earlier pact could be meaningless, shippers say, but with less than 80 days before the handover Taiwan and China remain sharply divided on some issues and have yet to decide even when and where to meet.

"We are not sure whether the mainland side will politicise the Taiwan-Hong Kong shipping negotiation," Fu Don-cheng, an official at Taiwan's policymaking Mainland Affairs Council, was quoted by the newspapers as saying.
Fu cast doubt over previous optimistic comments made by the council's vice chairman Kao Koong-lian, who said Taiwan was confident it would resolve the Hong Kong shipping problem in April.
"Relations across the Taiwan Strait are rather complicated...the Mainland Affairs Council has not set a deadline to complete the negotiation," Fu said.

Taiwan has officially authorised Chang Liang-jen, deputy secretary-general of the semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation to undertake talks with Beijing-appointed negotiator, George Chao, chairman of Hong Kong Shipowners' Association.
The two sides remain at loggerheads over whether Taiwan and Hong Kong-registered ships can hoist national flags of Taiwan and China when entering each other's waters, the newspapers said.

Taiwan officials have urged Beijing not to let politics complicate the links when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control at midnight on June 30 after 150 years of British colonial rule, local papers said on Sunday.

Fu told reporters Taiwan wants to "simplify" the sensitive sovereignty issue by allowing ships to lower all flags and identify themselves through telex communications before entering each other's waters.
Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war split them in 1949. Beijing regards the island as a rebel-held province that must be brought under its sovereignty.
Taiwan bars vessels flying communist China's red five-star, while those flying Taiwan's Republic of China flag are unwelcome in mainland ports.

The Hong Kong association has proposed that Hong Kong registered ships fly the Special Administrative Region flag when entering Taiwan waters. Taiwan ships should hoist their "plum blossom" flag, which is Taiwan's emblem, instead of the flag of Taiwan's government while in Hong Kong waters.
Hong Kong's post-handover constitution states that after July 1 Hong Kong-registered ships on international routes must fly China's national flag along with the SAR flag.
Taiwan firms, which have urged Taipei to secure direct shipping links with Hong Kong to ensure there is no interruption of service after the handover, said time is running short.

"I feel that when the government makes a policy, it often disregards the matter's urgency and the policy is not forward-looking," Hsu Wei-chen, a shipping company representative told a seminar in Taipei.

Hong Kong is the main transit point for the more than US$30 billion in Taiwan investments that have poured into China since the late 1980s, when a political thaw unleashed an explosion of unofficial Taiwan-China ties.
Taiwan said on Friday it would allow four shipping firms from China to sail directly across the Taiwan strait.
Taipei does not regard the new service as a "direct shipping link" but rather an "offshore transshipment" scheme because mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs.
Rather, they can be processed in an "offshore" bonded zone in Kaohsiung outside of customs for onward shipment.
Taipei's conditions seek to ensure the breakthrough does not undermine the sovereignty of the island's exiled Republic of China, which does not recognise the communists' sovereignty.
